newsitem.title: CANADA: Quebec voters divided on issue of partition.
newsitem.headline: Quebec voters divided on issue of partition.

text.p: Quebec voters are divided on the principle of whether the province can be partitioned if it separates from Canada, according to a Southam News-COMPAS poll published on Thursday.
On the question: "If Quebec has the right to separate, do Quebec's regions also?" half of Quebec respondents, including 45 percent of francophones, said yes, and the other half no.
In the rest of Canada, 80 percent of respondents said yes, while 20 percent said no, said Southam's English-language Montreal Gazette newspaper.

In the poll, 75 percent of Quebec respondents, including 72 percent of francophones, supported the right of northern Quebec's Cree and Inuit aboriginal peoples to remain in Canada if Quebec voted to separate in a future referendum on sovereignty.

In the October 1995 referendum, Quebec voted 50.6 percent to 49.4 percent against sovereignty. In separate referendums, Quebec's Cree and Inuit voted more than 90 percent against Quebec separation and indicated they would want to remain part of Canada should Quebec secede.

The figures were drawn from a cross-Canada survey conducted May 1-7. Results identified in the Gazette article were drawn from a core survey of 600 respondents in Quebec and 800 in the rest of Canada.

The responses in Quebec were considered accurate within 4.1 percentage points, 19 times out of 20. In the rest of Canada, results were considered accurate to within 3.5 percentage points, 19 times out of 20.

The poll suggested that if Quebec voters believed voting for separation would result in the division of the French-speaking province's vast territory, they would be much less likely to vote for sovereignty, the Gazette said.

So far, 31 Quebec municipalities, mainly on the island of Montreal and in the Outaouais region near Ottawa, have passed resolutions indicating they would want to remain part of Canada should Quebec separate.

The principle of partition raises the possibility that there could be great pressure to divide Quebec after separation, keeping Montreal -- a metropolis of three million people -- and much of the resource-rich north within Canada.
Quebec separatists, including the Parti Quebecois government, have dismissed the notion of partition, saying that a separate Quebec would not be divisible.
